titles.671: Man. Post. Cap. X: PLAC — if the pre-law world-sin is not the act, what is it?
titles.672: Man. Post. Cap. X: PLAC — then only reatus? Show ἁμαρτία used for bare guilt in Scripture
titles.673: Man. Post. Cap. X: PLAC — what of real corruption until the law? That helps Pighius/Pelagius
titles.674: Man. Post. Cap. X: PLAC — corruption plus double reatus is unexampled as ‘sin’
titles.675: Man. Post. Cap. X: PLAC — Paul adds ἄχρι νόμου; Calvin: the doubt was only before the law
titles.676: Man. Post. Cap. X tip — so Paul speaks of post-law-obvious sin; not Adam’s immediately imputed act

latin.671: PLAC. Cum igitur Apostolus loquatur de peccato quod usque ad legem fuit in mundo, quid per illud peccatum intelligendum est? Actus? Minime: fatetur enim Vir doctus illum non durasse usque ad legem, cum momento transierit.
latin.672: Reatus? Igitur per peccatum quod usque ad legem duravit in mundo, solus reatus intelligendus est. Detur igitur nobis locus aliquis e Novo Testamento in quo ἁμαρτία pro solo reatu usurpetur; aut detur saltem aliquis e Veteri, ubi sic usurpetur, cum de Dei iudicio agitur. Cur enim hoc loco vox illa, tam frequens, acciperetur sensu prorsus inusitato? Hoc primum.
latin.673: Deinde quid fiet de corruptione quae vere peccatum est, & revera fuit in omnibus hominibus usque ad legem? Quid est cur peccati nomine hoc loco, pro Apostoli more, non debeat intelligi? Potuitne Vir doctus quicquam comminisci, quod magis causam Pighii, imo Pelagii, iuvaret?
latin.674: Quod si dicas, peccatum quod usque ad legem in mundo fuit, una cum reatu corruptionem complecti, quem intelligas reatum quaeram: illumne qui sequitur corruptionem (peccatum enim, cum sit, reatum a se fundit), an vero illum qui corruptionem antecedere dicitur, & cuius respectu corruptio non est peccatum, sed poena peccati? Ille certe excludi non potest: intelligetur igitur corruptio duplici stipata reatu, altero antecedente, altero subsequente, quomodo peccatum recipi aliquando, nullo exemplo probari potest.
latin.675: Huic argumento accedat alterum hinc petitum, quod Apostolus non simpliciter dicit peccatum fuisse in mundo, sed addit ἄχρι νόμου, usque ad legem. Intelligit autem proculdubio legem Mosis, quam versu 20. praeterea ingressam ut abundaret peccatum docet. Itaque loco ἄχρι νόμου dixit versu sequente μέχρι Μωϋσέως, usque ad Mosen. Cur autem Apostolus illud usurpaviti usque ad legem, non usque ad Mosen? Nempe, ut verbis utar Calvini, dubitari poterat anne ante legem esset peccatum in mundo. Post legem fuisse minime dubium erat. Tantum haerebat quaestio in tempore legem praecedente. Satis igitur fuit probare peccatum fuisse in mundo ab Adam usque ad legem.
latin.676: Loquitur ergo Apostolus de peccato quod post legem ita patuit in mundo esse ut probatione non egeret. Atqui primum illud peccatum actuale Adami fuisse omnibus hominibus imputatum immediate tam post latam legem Mosis quam ante obscurum fuit. De eo igitur Apostolus non loquitur.

pass_a.671: Placeus turns GAR.3 back: Paul speaks of the sin that was in the world until the law—so what is that sin? The act? No: the learned man himself grants the act did not last until the law, since it passed in a moment.
pass_a.672: Then bare guilt? If so, the enduring pre-law world-sin is only reatus. Give even one NT place—or at least an OT judgment-text—where ἁμαρτία means bare guilt alone. Why take so common a word here in a wholly unused sense? That first.
pass_a.673: Next: what of the corruption that truly is sin and really was in all men until the law? Why should Paul’s usual ‘sin’ not mean that here? Could the learned man invent anything that helps Pighius—even Pelagius—more?
pass_a.674: If you say the pre-law world-sin packs corruption together with reatus, which reatus? The one that follows corruption (sin pours guilt from itself), or the alleged antecedent reatus that makes corruption a penalty rather than sin? The latter cannot be shut out—so you get corruption flanked by two guilts, prior and following: a way of taking ‘sin’ no example proves.
pass_a.675: A second proof: Paul does not merely say sin was in the world; he adds ἄχρι νόμου. He means Moses’ law (v.20: the law entered that sin might abound), and next says μέχρι Μωϋσέως. Why ‘until the law’ not ‘until Moses’? Calvin: one could doubt whether there was sin before the law; after the law it was undoubted—the question stuck only on the pre-law time. Enough, then, to prove sin from Adam to the law.
pass_a.676: So Paul speaks of a sin so plain after the law that it needs no proof. But that Adam’s first actual sin was immediately imputed to all—before and after Moses’ law—was obscure. Therefore Paul is not speaking of that.

671: PLAC. Since, then, the Apostle speaks of the sin which was in the world until the law, what is to be understood by that sin?
The act? By no means: for the learned man confesses that it did not last until the law, since it passed in a moment.
672: Guilt? Therefore by the sin which lasted in the world until the law, bare guilt alone is to be understood.
Let there be given us, then, some place from the New Testament in which ἁμαρτία is used for bare guilt alone; or at least some place from the Old, where it is so used when God’s judgment is in view.
For why in this place should that word, so frequent, be taken in a sense altogether unused?
673: Next, what will become of the corruption which truly is sin, and really was in all men until the law?
What reason is there why it ought not to be understood under the name of sin in this place, after the Apostle’s manner?
Could the learned man invent anything that would more help the cause of Pighius—nay, of Pelagius?
674: But if you say that the sin which was in the world until the law embraces corruption together with guilt, I will ask which guilt you mean: that which follows corruption (for sin, when it is, pours guilt from itself), or that which is said to precede corruption, and in respect of which corruption is not sin but the penalty of sin?

That latter certainly cannot be excluded: corruption will therefore be understood as attended with a double guilt, one antecedent, the other subsequent—a way of taking sin which can be proved by no example.
675: To this argument let another be added, drawn from this: that the Apostle does not simply say sin was in the world, but adds ἄχρι νόμου, until the law.
And he no doubt means the law of Moses, which in verse 20 he teaches entered besides, that sin might abound.
And so in place of ἄχρι νόμου he said in the following verse μέχρι Μωϋσέως, until Moses.
But why did the Apostle use ‘until the law,’ not ‘until Moses’?
Namely, to use Calvin’s words, it could be doubted whether there was sin in the world before the law.
That there was after the law was not at all doubtful.
The question stuck only on the time preceding the law.
It was therefore enough to prove that sin was in the world from Adam until the law.
676: The Apostle therefore speaks of the sin which after the law was so plain in the world that it did not need proof.
But that that first actual sin of Adam was immediately imputed to all men, as much after Moses’ law was given as before, was obscure.
Of that, therefore, the Apostle is not speaking.

671.choice: Pre-law world-sin cannot be the momentary act

673.choice: Real corruption until the law fits Paul’s ‘sin’

675.choice: Paul targets the doubted pre-law span (Calvin)

676.choice: Paul’s plain post-law sin ≠ obscure immediate Adam-act

676.note: sin needing no proof after the law
